title: Two Pointers
summary: Walk two indexes through one or two sequences so each element is visited a constant number of times.
lesson:
How it works
- Keep two indexes and move one or both on every step based on what they point at.
- Opposite ends: start at both ends of one sequence and move inward until they meet.
- Same direction: a slow index marks where the next kept element goes while a fast index scans.
- Two inputs: one index per sequence, advancing whichever side should be consumed next.

When to reach for it
- The input is sorted, or symmetric questions compare the front with the back.
- You must rearrange or filter an array in place with `O(1)` extra space.
- You are merging or comparing two already-ordered sequences.

Common patterns
- Palindrome-style checks compare `left` and `right` and skip characters that do not count.
- Read/write compaction copies kept elements to the write index, then fills the rest.
- Merge steps pick the smaller head of two sorted inputs, then append whatever remains.
- Digit-by-digit arithmetic walks both numbers from their last position and carries between steps.

Pitfalls
- Off-by-one loop conditions: decide whether the pointers may meet (`<` versus `<=`).
- Forgetting the leftover tail after one input runs out.
- Skipping logic that can run past the end of the array; recheck bounds inside inner loops.
- Every pointer must move on every iteration or the loop never ends.
